info.name: Relay
info.description:
End-to-end collection for the Relay messenger.

## Before you run

Start infrastructure and services:

```
docker compose up -d                     # keycloak, kafka, postgres x4, redis
(cd eureka && ./gradlew bootRun)         # :8761
(cd api-gateway && ./gradlew bootRun)    # :8080
(cd auth && ./gradlew bootRun)           # random port, reached via the gateway
(cd user && ./gradlew bootRun --args='--server.port=8085')
(cd message && ./gradlew bootRun --args='--server.port=8084')
(cd notification && ./gradlew bootRun)
(cd websocket-gateway && ./gradlew bootRun)  # :8083
```

`user` and `message` ship with `server.port: 0`, so they get a random port and are
normally reached only through Eureka. This collection calls their `/internal` endpoints
directly, which needs a fixed port — hence the `--server.port` overrides above. Change the
`userServiceUrl` / `messageServiceUrl` variables if you prefer different ones.

Keycloak must have the `relay-realm` realm, a `relay-client` client with the secret in
`auth/src/main/resources/application.yaml`, and a client role named `USER`.

## How to run

Use **Run collection** — the folders are ordered and later requests depend on variables
captured by earlier ones (tokens, user ids, dialog ids). Running requests one by one works
too, as long as you go top to bottom.

## WebSocket

Postman collections cannot carry WebSocket requests, so the socket is not in here. All frames
use the versioned envelope of ARCHITECTURE.md §10: `{"v":1,"type":"<dot.name>","id":"<uuid>",
"ts":<epoch-ms>,"payload":{...}}` with snake_case payload keys. The envelope `id` of a
`message.send` IS the client message id (idempotency + ack correlation).

**1. Postman native WebSocket request** — New > WebSocket, URL `ws://localhost:8083/ws`.
Under *Protocols* add two entries: `access_token` and then your access token value. Connect,
then send:

```json
{"v":1,"type":"ping","id":"p-1"}
{"v":1,"type":"message.send","id":"<uuid>","ts":1730000000000,"payload":{"dialog_id":"<dialogId>","text":"hello"}}
```

**2. Browser console** on any page:

```js
const jwt = '<paste accessTokenA>';
const ws = new WebSocket('ws://localhost:8083/ws', ['access_token', jwt]);
ws.onmessage = e => console.log(e.data);
ws.onopen = () => ws.send(JSON.stringify({v:1, type:'ping', id:'p-1'}));
// then:
// ws.send(JSON.stringify({v:1, type:'message.send', id:crypto.randomUUID(), ts:Date.now(),
//                         payload:{dialog_id:'<dialogId>', text:'hi'}}))
```

The token rides in the subprotocol list rather than the URL, so it stays out of access logs and
browser history. Expect `session.connected` first; a send is answered with `ack` (correlated by
`client_msg_id` = your envelope id) once the message is persisted — the send travels
gateway → Kafka `messages.incoming` → message-service → Postgres → Kafka `messages.delivery` →
gateway. Recipients (including your own other devices) get `message.new`. Failures come back as
`error` frames whose `ref_id` echoes your envelope id — that is the cue to retry the same id
over the REST fallback. To watch delivery between two users, open a second socket as user B and
send as user A.

item.name: 2.1 Profile, avatar and contacts (through api-gateway)
item.description:
The client-facing user surface. The profile is replaced with `PUT` and a complete body — the DTO is the editable projection, deliberately smaller than what `GET /me` returns. Every "my" endpoint takes the caller from the JWT's `sub`, never from the path or the body, so there is no request here that can touch somebody else's profile or address book.

Contacts are a one-sided address book: adding B does not add A to B's list and does not ask B to accept. Adding twice answers 200 instead of 201 rather than failing, because a retry is not a mistake.

## Avatar upload

Postman cannot carry a binary fixture, so the multipart upload is not in here. With `accessTokenA` from folder 1 (Postman shows it in *Variables*):

```
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/user/me/avatar \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -F file=@/path/to/photo.png
```

The response carries `avatarUrl` — a relative `/api/v1/user/{id}/avatar?v=<millis>`, because the host depends on which edge the client came through. `v` changes whenever the picture does, so caches cannot serve a stale face. The stored content type comes from the file's own signature, not from the `Content-Type` you send: PNG, JPEG, WebP and GIF are accepted, up to 1 MiB, and anything else (an SVG, say, which is a script-bearing document) is refused with 415.

request.description: PUT replaces the editable projection of the profile — both names, as one. It is narrower than what `GET /me` returns on the same URI: `email` doubles as the Keycloak username, `avatarUrl` is set by uploading a picture, and the password lives in Keycloak (folder 5.1). Sending back a stale value overwrites whatever another of your devices changed in between; two fields wide is the accepted price of an unambiguous verb.
`@NotBlank`, not `@Size(min = 1)` — the latter counts three spaces as a valid name, and a profile with a blank name renders as an empty row in every client.
Bean Validation (`@Size(max = 128)`) rejects it before the service is reached.

item.name: 3. Message service (internal)
item.description:
Dialog membership is resolved server-side and ends up as `recipientIds` on the `messages.delivery` event, which is what the websocket gateway fans out on. A client never names its own recipients.

The `clientMessageId` requests below are the important ones: they demonstrate that a repeated send is recognised rather than stored twice, which is what makes a client's REST fallback safe after a lost socket acknowledgement.

item.name: 5. Notifications (device tokens + offline push)
item.description:
Step 2 of the offline-push flow. Register a device token as user B, then send a message to B while B has NO WebSocket open: the gateway publishes a request to the `notifications` topic and notification-service logs `PUSH (stub) -> user=... device=...` — the FCM adapter is stubbed until credentials exist. Watch it in the notification-service console, or inspect the topic in kafka-ui (http://localhost:8082).

These calls go through the api-gateway; notification-service validates the JWT itself and takes the token owner from its `sub` — you cannot register a device for someone else.

item.name: 5.1 Password change (auth + Keycloak)
item.description:
Changing a password is an auth concern, not a profile one: Keycloak owns the credential and user-db has no password column. It is the one authenticated endpoint on the auth service — the gateway lets all of `/api/v1/auth/**` through unauthenticated, so auth validates the JWT itself and takes the account from the `sub` claim.

The current password is required even though the caller already holds a valid token: otherwise a leaked access token would be enough to lock the owner out permanently. It is verified with a password grant, the only way to check a credential through Keycloak's API.

Existing sessions are deliberately left valid, so you are not signed out of the device you just used — which is why the last request here can still authenticate with the token captured before the change.
